title: Paul Skenes expects to make two starts in World Baseball Classic
content:
Pittsburgh Pirates right-hander Paul Skenes, the reigning National League Cy Young Award winner, is at a different stage of his career than Detroit Tigers lefty Tarik Skubal, who is coming off back-to-back AL Cy Youngs.

So perhaps not surprisingly, Skenes is approaching the World Baseball Classic differently than his AL counterpart, and planning to take on a greater workload for Team USA.

While Skubal told reporters Monday he will pitch only once in the WBC, Skenes said he expects to make two starts, assuming the U.S. advances out of pool play.

“We win, we go as far as we should, I’ll pitch again in the tournament,” Skenes said in an interview I conducted with him for Fox Sports.

Skenes, who is scheduled to make his Grapefruit League debut Wednesday against the Atlanta Braves, said he is also scheduled to pitch in one of Team USA’s exhibitions next week in Arizona. The U.S. will face the San Francisco Giants on Tuesday and Colorado Rockies on Wednesday before departing for WBC pool play in Houston.

Giants right-hander Logan Webb said he also expects to make two starts for Team USA, saying, “I’m gonna see it through, I’ll be there the whole time. I want to be there the whole time with the guys.”

Skubal agreed to pitch in the WBC after a conversation he had with Skenes at the Major League Baseball Players Association meetings this past December. But Skubal, who is entering his free-agent year, is at greater financial risk than Skenes, who has yet to reach salary arbitration and is under club control for four more seasons.

If Skubal, who will earn $32 million this season, stays healthy and pitches effectively, he could warrant $400 million on the open market. He is also pitching for a team that considers itself a World Series contender. The Pirates, while expected to improve, last made the postseason in 2015.

Skenes said when Team USA manager Mark DeRosa approached him in April about pitching in the WBC, he accepted immediately. He attended the U.S. Air Force Academy for two years before transferring to LSU, and told DeRosa he wanted to pitch in the WBC to honor U.S. servicemen and women.

“That’s what we do it for,” Skenes said. “This is the greatest country in the world. That’s what I believe. That’s why I wanted to serve, why I went to the Air Force Academy. And those folks don’t get the recognition they deserve.

“I’m not suiting up in my OCPs (Operational Camouflage Pattern uniforms) again or my dress blues or anything like that, but it is going to be a very cool experience for me personally. For (team captain) Aaron Judge to answer the call, all the guys on the position-player side and then all the pitchers that we’ve gotten, it’s this thing that’s a lot bigger than any of us.

“We’re doing it to represent the men and women that are fighting for us, along with many other things that make this country the greatest country in the world. That puts it into perspective a little bit.”
